videos.desc:
At 11:40 AM on August 9, 1864, seventy-five thousand pounds of gunpowder and thirty thousand artillery shells detonated at the waterfront of City Point, Virginia—the central supply depot sustaining the Union siege of Petersburg. 

The blast obliterated 180 feet of timber wharf, destroyed two supply warehouses, and showered the headquarters bluff of Lieutenant General Ulysses S. Grant with iron projectiles, killing an orderly paces from the general's tent.

videos.desc:
The last Civil War general died in 1938. The first one was already dead in July 1861.
They did not all die in battle. Confederate generals were more than twice as likely to be killed by wounds as Union generals. Most still outlived the war. They died from bullets, friendly fire, typhoid, hotel pistols, yellow fever, stroke, throat cancer, funeral rain, and a Petersburg wound that took fifty years to finish the job.

Instead, caution won out, and Lee escaped back into Virginia to fight for nearly two more years.

videos.desc:

He was, in Southern minds, just another general who’d break the way McClellan, Burnside, and Hooker had broken before him.

Grant did the one thing no general before him had done — and meant it.

Soldiers begged civilians for food. A newspaper ran out of paper and started printing on wallpaper. videos.title: What They Found in Congress's Filing Cabinet After 105 Years
videos.desc:
Robert E. Lee did something after the Civil War that history textbooks never told you. He signed a loyalty oath to the United States in 1865 and formally asked Congress to restore his citizenship. He did everything right. Filled out the paperwork. Signed it. Mailed it to Washington.

Congress lost it in a filing cabinet for 105 years.
